title: Analyzing autophagosomes and mitophagosomes in the mouse brain using electron microscopy
protocol: Conduct perfusion in a chemical fume hood.
Use perfusion buffer containing 10 units/mL heparin at warm room temperature (23°C–37°C).
Use fixative consisting of 4% paraformaldehyde and 2% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M PB at warm room temperature (23°C–37°C).
Anesthetize mice with isoflurane.
Inject mice intraperitoneally with ketamine (110 mg/kg) and xylazine (7 mg/kg).
Wait until adequate anesthesia is achieved as determined by loss of response to toe pinching.
Place the mouse on a shallow tray.
Make a small incision in the diaphragm beneath the rib cage using a pair of iris scissors.
Cut the diaphragm along the entire length of the rib cage to expose the pleural cavity.
Insert a blunt tip needle into the left ventricle of the heart.
Use a hemostat to clamp the heart to secure the needle and prevent leakage.
Cut open the right atrium with a pair of iris scissors.
Attach the needle base to a three-way valve connected to two 50-mL syringes, each containing 0.1 M PB with heparin or fixative.
Turn the valve to open the PB line and manually inject 25 mL 0.1 M PB with heparin within 1 min.
Switch the perfusion solution to fixative and manually inject 25 mL fixative within ∼4 min.
Isolate the brain.
Remove the head with a pair of scissors.
Expose the skull by making an incision along the midline from the neck to the nose.
Remove the vertebrae and muscles that remain attached to the skull.
Use the tip of a pair of iris scissors to carefully cut open the skull.
Lift up the blade when cutting to prevent damaging the brain.
Use a rongeur to peel the skull away from the dorsal surface of the brain.
Use a spatula to sever the olfactory bulbs and nerves connected to the ventral surface of the brain.
Place the isolated brain in fresh fixative overnight (12–18 h) at 4°C.
Prepare a 5% agarose block by adding 5 g agarose powder and 0.85 g NaCl to 100 mL Milli-Q or distilled water.
Heat the solution in a microwave oven until boiling.
Pour the agarose solution into several 10-cm tissue culture plates and let it cool down.
Cut the agarose block into 3 × 1 × 1.5 cm (L × W × H) cubes.
Wash brains with PBS three times for 20 minutes each.
Gently agitate brains during incubation with PBS.
Cut along the rostral border of the cerebellum using a razor blade to remove the cerebellum.
Place the brain on filter paper to dry the bottom surface slightly moist.
Glue the brain without the cerebellum to the sample holder against the agarose block using Krazy glue.
Orient the glued brain with the dorsoventral axis parallel to the holder plate and rostral tip facing up.
Fill the cutting chamber of the vibratome with PBS.
Cut 150-μm thick coronal sections from the brain.
Transfer brain sections into 6-well plates using a fine brush.
Wash the brain sections with 0.1 M cacodylate buffer three times for 5 minutes each.
Proceed to Step 3 directly if time permits; otherwise, keep brain sections at 4°C overnight and proceed on the next day.
Prepare fresh 1% osmium tetroxide solution by adding 250 μL of 4% osmium stock solution and 100 μL of 1 M cacodylate stock solution to Milli-Q or distilled water.
Bring the volume to 1 mL with Milli-Q or distilled water.
Remove cacodylate buffer from brain sections using a disposable transfer pipette.
Do not allow the brain sections to dry during any procedures in Step 3.
Add 1 mL of freshly made 1% osmium tetroxide solution to cover the sections, using a fresh pipette.
Incubate brain sections with the osmium tetroxide solution at room temperature (20°C–22°C) for 30 min in the dark.
Fix the tissue in the dark for a short time at room temperature.
Wash brain sections 3×10 min with 0.1 M cacodylate buffer.
Prepare 1% uranyl acetate solution by adding 0.01 g uranyl acetate to 1 mL of 50% ethanol.
Protect the 1% uranyl acetate solution from light.
Dehydrate brain sections with 50% ethanol (3×5 min).
Replace 50% ethanol with the 1% uranyl acetate in ethanol solution.
Keep brain sections in the 1% uranyl acetate solution for 15 min in the dark.
Continue to dehydrate brain sections with 75% ethanol (2×5 min), 95% ethanol (10 min), and 100% ethanol (3×10 min).
Transfer brain sections to propylene oxide in glass scintillation vials.
Change propylene oxide once after transfer.
Replace propylene oxide with a 1:1 mixture of epon and propylene oxide.
Incubate brain sections with the mixture for 1 h.
Replace the epon and propylene oxide mixture with epon.
Keep brain sections in epon at room temperature (20°C–22°C) overnight (12–18 h).
On the day after dehydration, replace the overnight epon with freshly-made epon.
Keep brain sections in epon for several hours (we keep them for 24 h) at room temperature (20°C–22°C).
Place dehydrated, epon infiltrated tissues between two Aclar sheets separated by a thin layer of epon to make an Aclar sandwich.
Avoid trapping bubbles in the sandwich and cure it in an oven set at 64°C for 48 h to complete the embedding procedure.
Mount flat bottom embedding capsules on a corresponding polypropylene capsule holder.
Pour the epon into the capsules and heat in an oven as above.
Remove one Aclar sheet.
Outline the amygdala under a light microscope using a marker pen.
Carve out the outlined amygdala with a scalpel.
Scratch one end of the epon cylinder in a grid pattern with a razor blade to assist adhesion.
Glue the epon-embedded amygdala to the center of the grid with one drop of Krazy glue on the side still covered with Aclar material.
Ensure the tissue is flat and avoid using excessive glue.
Dry the cylinder mounted with the tissue at room temperature overnight (12–18 hours).
Trim the edges of the tissue to make it a trapezoid, ensuring not to damage the tissue.
Wipe off any debris from the cylinder with wet paper towels.
Use wood handles derived from cotton swabs to transfer epon-embedded tissues onto Alcar sheets.
Place one end of the second Alcar sheet on the first sheet and slowly lay down the rest to avoid bubbles.
Cut thick brain sections from the face of the mounted tissue block using an ultramicrotome until the entire tissue face is exposed.
Stain sections with a toluidine blue solution.
Continue staining on a hot plate until the solution is dried.
Examine thick sections under a light microscope to determine the proper area for electron microscope examination.
Cut ultrathin brain sections (60 nm) from the face of mounted brain tissue using an ultramicrotome.
Mount the ultrathin sections on formvar/carbon-coated single-slot copper grids.
Alternatively, mount the ultrathin sections on nickel grids.
Store grids in a grid box in a desiccator until use.
Cut sections about 1-μm thick in the ultramicrotome.
Mount 1-μm thick sections on glass slides.
Stain mounted sections with a toluidine blue solution for visualization.
Go to low magnification (50–100×) on the electron microscope.
Mark off boundaries of the brain region on the ultrathin section being imaged.
Correlate the image on the Gatan camera screen with an image of the last 1 μm section taken before the ultrathin sections.
Cut ultrathin sections (60 nm) when the proper region is reached in the ultramicrotome.
Mount ultrathin sections on formvar/carbon-coated single slot grids.
Mount grids on a Hiraoka grid support plate.
Stain with 0.3% lead citrate solution for 3 minutes.
Wash the stained grids three times with distilled water.
Dry the grids using a pipette and then with filter paper edges.
Store grids in a grid box until use.
Place a grid containing a brain section into a holder.
Insert the holder into a JEOL JEM-2100 transmission electron microscope.
Align and examine the sample at 200 kV.
Go to low magnification (50–100×).
Compare the image on the Gatan camera monitor screen with an image of the last 1 μm section taken before the ultrathin sections.
Mark off the boundaries of the brain region on the ultrathin section to be imaged, using the JEOL specimen position display window.
Take images at high magnifications (2,500× to 25,000×).
